## The question, frozen

The title and opening make one question central: **what principles should guide the design of Internet protocols?** (The document also asks "is there an architecture?"; that serves this one.) Range: the public Internet, at the inter-networking layer, during the document's snapshot period. What is asked: what to do when designing or judging a design. It is a design question, not a causal one. Frozen there.

## Jobs and parts

Jobs, all named by the owner (**given**): connectivity across unlike hardware (J1); scale to millions (J2); interoperation among rival vendors and providers (J3); survive partial failure (J4); keep evolving as technology changes (J5); end-user security (J6); unambiguous endpoints (J7).

Parts: the numbered principles. Two are load-bearing beams: the end-to-end argument (2.3) and "constant change" (1, 2.4).

## Part by part

| Part(s) | Mark |
|---|---|
| 2.3 end-to-end; fate-sharing; datagrams over virtual circuits | **Held** — by J4. Remove it and no middle box can carry end-to-end integrity; the reason is inside (only endpoints hold the needed state). Also **borrowed** — it rests on Saltzer's argument, which is not tested here. |
| 2.2 one protocol; 3.2 choose one way; 6.5 mandate one algorithm; 6.3 label algorithms; 5.3 full conformance | **Held** — by J3. Without one common thing, vendors and providers cannot meet. |
| 3.3 scale readily | **Held** — by J2. |
| 3.1 heterogeneity; 3.12 self-describing objects | **Held** — by J1. |
| 4.4, 4.5 unambiguous addresses | **Held** — by J7. |
| 3.14 running code first; 3.11 no circular dependencies; 4.1 avoid hard-coded addresses; 2.4 consensus and running code | **Held** — by J5. 3.11 carries its reason inside (routing must not lean on DNS), so its limit is held too. In 2.4 the held part is "running code," which you can look at; "rough consensus" is not measurable, so it is looser than it reads. |
| 6.2 user-responsibility; 6.4 time-tested algorithms | **Held** — by J6. 6.4's hold is a selection argument (fitted provenance). |
| 3.4 performance and cost; 3.5 keep it simple; 3.6 modularity; 3.13 shared notation; 4.3 case-independent ASCII | **Loose** — a near neighbour ("most maintainable," "layered," "case-sensitive names") does the job as well. Nothing would look different. |
| 5.2 export controls secondary | **Held if** — held only by the asserted claim that all required technology can be made in every country. That claim is not tested here. |
| 6.1 fit IP security architecture | **Fixed** — set by the owner, not tested. |

## Whole-explanation checks

**Where the parts came from.** Most are **fitted**: "found useful in the past," drawn from 25 years of practice. A few are **built** — 2.3 from Saltzer's argument, 3.11 from the DNS case. A few are **asserted**: 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, and 5.2's fabrication claim.

**Flip.** Mostly it is a list of advice, not one outcome. But note 2.1 gives both sides ("no architecture, only tradition") and then keeps them apart, which is fair rather than loose.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** "Connectivity is its own reward" leans on network growth as its evidence. Growth is a fitted signpost, not a forced step, so this part is looser than stated.

**Pairs that pull.** 3.8 ("avoid options and parameters") pulls against 6.3 ("permit alternative algorithms"). "Tolerant when receiving" (3.9) pulls against end-user security (6.2) — tolerating malformed input is how holes open. The document keeps both sides and does not say which gives way.

**Catch-alls and gauges.** "Engineering feedback is more important than any architectural principles" (2.4) can absorb any failure of any principle above. Its gauge is "running code," which is real but weak — it would not show *which* principle failed.

**Change list.** Wide and honest: new media, failure, scale, new requirements, competition, export controls, compromise. It states its limit up front (a snapshot). That is the right move. Parts 3.4–3.6, 3.13 and 4.3 state no limit and carry no gauge.

**Rival.** The intelligent network (telephone/ATM style) that does end-to-end work in the middle. The change that tells them apart is partial failure, and it does — so the end-to-end beam survives and the rival is real.

## What would make it harder to vary

1. Settle 3.8 against 6.3: say which yields when a design needs both no options and swappable algorithms. That single line would hold a whole class of cases.
2. Give 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6 a gauge (something measurable that would show they earned their place), or drop them to "free choices," said plainly.

## What this does not show

Passing is not truth. These are guidelines that stick their neck out; some parts are held, some are habits.

## One next step

Take 3.8 and 6.3 and write down, for one protocol, which one gives way — that is the cheapest test the document has left open.
